newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian vote light but trouble-free.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian vote light but trouble-free.

text.p: Heavily-armed NATO troops oversaw trouble-free voting in Bosnia's first post-war national elections on Saturday but few Moslem refugees risked crossing into Serb territory to cast ballots in their former homes.

Those who made the journey across the ethnic divide between the Bosnian Serb republic and the Moslem-Croat federation were shepherded in buses by NATO peacekeepers and U.N. police to pre-arranged voting stations.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which set up the elections, said early voting was moderate but international mediators were relieved by the absence of confrontation.
OSCE mission chief Robert Frowick told reporters in Sarajevo:" The day is not yet over ... but overall, so far, things are going pretty well."
The elections were designed to give Bosnia democratic inter-ethnic institutions and re-knit ties between its Moslem, Serb and Croat communities after 43 months of war.

Although the likeliest outcome was a victory for the three main nationalist parties which led the country into conflict, international mediators were encouraged by a pledge of future cooperation from Bosnian Serb hardliners.

Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic told U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke her separatist Serb Democratic Party (SDS) would not boycott the new collective presidency where it will have a seat along with Moslem and Croat representatives.
The SDS candidate is Momcilo Krajisnik, a senior member of the Bosnian Serb war leadership and a strong supporter of Bosnian Serb independence from the Moslem-Croat federation.
Holbrooke, whose diplomacy succeeded in ending the war last year, cautiously welcomed Plavsic's promise and added:
"We have got to see Krajisnik, if he wins, come to Sarajevo. I don't believe anything until it happens but the fact is that this is one of the major next steps."
Although polling was free of violence, incomplete voting lists caused chaos in some areas and the OSCE said would be extended for three hours in some areas and possibly into Sunday.
A Serb voter in Bijeljina complained he was left off the electoral roll but found the name of his father who died 18 years ago.

Almost three million electors were eligible to vote for the collective Bosnian national presidency and parliament, a president and national assembly for the Serb republic and an assembly and cantonal administrations for the federation.
Many of the Moslems who decided to vote in the Serb republic were lured by the opportunity to see homes from which they were ethnically cleansed when the war began in 1992.
There was scant political point in their going back since municipal elections which should also have been held on Saturday were postponed until November.
Only a handful of Moslems went back to vote in the area of Srebrenica where several thousand unarmed Moslem prisoners were massacred by the Bosnian Serb army after its capture last year.

One group of 21 who did make the journey and voted in the hardline nationalist town of Bratunac near Srebrenica said they were treated politely by the Serbs who included former neighbours who had helped drive them out.
"I came to see my Bratunac. I just wanted them to let us come back," said 64-year-old Ibrahim Hodzic. "I am voting today because I wanted to see my town up close. I hope it won't be the last time."
Thousands of Bosnian Serb refugees from Moslem-Croat territory were taken by bus and train from neighbouring Yugoslavia to Serb republic towns in north Bosnia to vote.
One elderly Serb refugee from Sarajevo who came from Belgrade said the outcome was predictable.
"Everyone's going to vote for their own family," he said in a reference to the nationalist parties.
Pitched against the prospects for unification are the ethnic animosities left by a war which killed an estimated 200,000 people, drove many more from their homes and devastated Bosnia's main towns.

One elderly Serb refugee was heard saying to a friend outside a polling station in Vlasenica in eastern Bosnia: "All (Moslems) should be exterminated for good. We didn't fight this bloody war so Moslems could vote in Bosnia."
